title: Gulf Flight Chaos Deepens as Europe Extends Airspace Ban Through August
excerpt: EASA has extended its advisory warning airlines to avoid airspace over the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and parts of Oman until August 31, as the US-Iran conflict continues to disrupt one of the world's busiest aviation corridors.
body:
• The European Union Aviation Safety Agency extended its Gulf conflict zone advisory until August 31, 2026, covering five countries and parts of Oman
  • IATA estimates 46% of Gulf flights have been removed from the global inventory since the US-Iran conflict began
  • British Airways, Lufthansa Group and other European carriers have suspended Gulf routes through October, forcing lengthy detours for Europe-Asia flights
  • Emirates, Etihad and Air Arabia continue to cancel Kuwait-bound services as Kuwait International Airport operates under tight restrictions

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency has extended its conflict zone advisory for Gulf airspace through August 31, warning airlines to avoid flying over the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and parts of Oman at all altitudes. The move underscores how deeply the US-Iran conflict has disrupted commercial aviation across one of the world's most critical air corridors.

The advisory, designated CZIB-2026-07R1, cites "unpredictable military developments, combined with the possible use of missiles, drones, combat aircraft and air-defense systems" as posing a high risk to civilian flights. Separate bulletins already in effect instruct airlines to avoid Iranian, Iraqi and Lebanese airspace entirely.

According to IATA, 46% of Gulf flights have been removed from the global inventory since open conflict between the United States and Iran erupted in late February 2026. None of the major carriers have returned to full capacity.

European Carriers Pull Back

The advisory applies to all EU operators and third-country carriers flying to, from or within the European Union. Major European airlines have responded by suspending or drastically scaling back Gulf services:

British Airways has suspended flights to Dubai, Bahrain and Amman until October 25, while cutting Doha service to once daily from August 1 and permanently dropping Jeddah. The Lufthansa Group — including Swiss, Austrian Airlines and Brussels Airlines — has suspended Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Riyadh, Muscat and several other Middle Eastern destinations until October 24. KLM and Air France have also pulled back from Dubai and Riyadh.

The suspensions have forced flights between Europe and the Asia-Pacific region into lengthy southern detours, adding hours of flight time and significant operational costs.

Kuwait Routes Hit Hardest

Within the Gulf, Kuwait-bound services have borne the brunt of disruptions. Kuwait International Airport has been operating under tight restrictions for much of 2026, following drone and rocket incidents linked to the wider Iran-US confrontation.

Emirates cancelled eight flights between Dubai and Kuwait over a recent weekend. Etihad suspended Abu Dhabi-Kuwait flights EY653 and EY654, citing operational reasons. Air Arabia cancelled multiple Sharjah-Kuwait and Abu Dhabi-Kuwait services.

Passengers report receiving last-minute notifications that Kuwait segments have been removed from their itineraries even while longer-haul legs remain intact, effectively stranding the Kuwait portion of their journey.

"According to IATA, 46% of Gulf flights have been removed from the global inventory since open conflict between the United States and Iran erupted in late February 2026."

Gradual Recovery, Fragile Outlook

Most Gulf airspaces, including those over the UAE, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Oman, have progressively reopened with managed corridors and heightened risk assessments. Daily flight data shows the three major Gulf carriers — Emirates, Etihad and Qatar Airways — operated a combined 1,026 flights on June 7, down from peaks above 1,100 but stabilised from mid-May lows below 800.

EASA acknowledged the improvement but warned that "the sustainability of the ceasefire remains uncertain in the longer term, with a possibility of rapid escalation." The agency said that should the existing truce break down, the affected airspaces would be "exposed to imminent threats."

What's Next

For Indian travellers and the large diaspora community in the Gulf, the disruptions mean continued uncertainty around travel between the UAE, India and Europe. Airlines are offering free rebooking and full refunds under EU261 passenger-rights rules, but full restoration of pre-conflict route networks remains distant — particularly for transcontinental flights that once relied on central Middle Eastern corridors. Passengers are urged to check flight status directly with airlines before heading to the airport.
nri_angle: Indian expats in the UAE form one of the largest diaspora communities in the Gulf, and ongoing flight disruptions directly impact their ability to visit family in India and travel to Europe.
author: Diaspora Desk
